prompt: Write an email to a colleague about doing every task well, however small. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: A small thought on doing the little things well

Hi Sam,

I've been meaning to write this for a while. Something you did last week has stayed with me, and I wanted to tell you about it.

After the quarterly review, you went back and tidied the shared project notes. No one asked you to. You fixed the broken links, put the headings in order, and added a short summary at the top. It took you maybe twenty minutes, and nobody will ever thank you for it. But when I opened the document the next morning, I found what I needed in under a minute. It saved me real time, and I suspect it saved others the same.

That got me thinking about how much of our work is made of small tasks like that one. A reply to a customer. A line in a status report. A file name. A handoff note. It's easy to treat these as filler between the "real" work, and to do them quickly and carelessly so we can get on to something more important. But I've come to believe the small tasks are where most of our reputation is built. People rarely see the big project in full. They see whether you answered their email clearly, whether your numbers were labeled, whether you did what you said you'd do by Friday.

There is also a quieter benefit. When I do small things carefully, the habit carries over. Care is not something I can switch on only for high-stakes moments. If I let myself be sloppy on the minor stuff, I notice that sloppiness creeping into the major stuff too. Doing small things well keeps my standards steady, so I don't have to summon them in a crisis.

Doing every task well doesn't mean being a perfectionist. I'm not suggesting we spend an hour polishing a two-line message. It means giving each task the attention it actually needs, finishing it properly, and not leaving a mess for the next person. Often that's just one more read-through, or one more sentence of context so the reader isn't left guessing.

I try to ask myself a simple question before I call something done: if someone else picked this up tomorrow, would they be glad or frustrated? Most of the time that's enough to tell me whether to stop or to spend another few minutes.

I wanted you to know that your tidy notes were noticed, and that this kind of care is exactly what makes you a pleasure to work with. Please keep doing it.

If you're free Thursday, I'd love to grab coffee and hear how you approach this. I suspect I could learn a few things from you.

Thanks again,
[name]
